720° is the SUM of all six interior angles. Each one is 720 ÷ 6 = 120°.

cp-parallel-through-point__mcq.prompt: Copying the angle from Q up to P guarantees the lines are parallel because…

options.label: equal corresponding angles imply the lines are parallel
options.feedback: When a transversal makes equal corresponding angles with two lines, those lines are parallel — the construction manufactures exactly that equality.

options.label: P and Q are the same distance apart as the lines
options.feedback: Distance between the points isn't what's copied — the ANGLE is. Equal corresponding angles are what force parallelism.

options.label: the transversal is perpendicular to both lines
options.feedback: The transversal is a slanted line, not a perpendicular. Parallelism follows from the equal angles it makes, whatever their size.

options.label: any two lines through P and Q are parallel
options.feedback: Most such lines cross. Only when the corresponding angles MATCH do the two lines stay parallel.

cp-parallel-through-point__mcq.prompt: Through a point P not on line ℓ, how many lines can be drawn parallel to ℓ?

options.label: exactly one
options.feedback: The construction builds one; any other line through P makes a different angle with the transversal and so must meet ℓ. Existence and uniqueness together.

options.label: none — a point off the line blocks all parallels
options.feedback: The construction just drew one, so at least one exists. "None" is ruled out immediately.

options.label: infinitely many, fanning out from P
options.feedback: Only the line with the MATCHING corresponding angle stays parallel; every other tilt crosses ℓ. Just one qualifies.

options.label: exactly two, one on each side
options.feedback: Both "sides" through P with the right angle are the SAME line. There is a single parallel, not a pair.

cp-parallel-through-point__numeric.prompt: Across the same two parallel lines, the CO-INTERIOR (same-side interior) angle to that 55° angle measures how many degrees?

commonErrors.feedback: 55° would make them EQUAL — that's the alternate/corresponding relationship. Co-interior angles are SUPPLEMENTARY: 180 − 55 = 125°.
305° comes from 360 − 55 — a full-turn idea. Co-interior angles sum to a straight angle: 180 − 55 = 125°.

cp-perp-at-point__mcq.prompt: What guarantees PQ ⊥ the line, without measuring?

options.label: Both P and Q are equidistant from A and B, so PQ is the perpendicular bisector of AB
options.feedback: Two points equally far from A and B pin down AB's perpendicular bisector — and it meets AB at 90° through the midpoint P.

options.label: Q was drawn directly above P by eye
options.feedback: Nothing was placed by eye — Q is fixed by two equal-radius arcs. Its being on the perpendicular follows from equidistance, not from looking straight.

options.label: The compass always makes right angles
options.feedback: A compass makes CIRCLES, not right angles. The 90° comes from the equidistance argument, not the tool itself.

options.label: Because PA = PB, angle APQ must be 90°
options.feedback: PA = PB only makes P the midpoint — it doesn't force the angle. The second pair of equal arcs (giving Q) is what squares the corner.

cp-perp-at-point__mcq.prompt: Raising a perpendicular at a point on a line is secretly the same as…

options.label: bisecting the straight angle at that point
options.feedback: The line is a 180° angle at P; the perpendicular splits it into two 90° halves — an angle bisection.

options.label: copying a segment
options.feedback: Copying a segment reproduces a LENGTH elsewhere — no angle is created. Here we're halving an angle, not moving a length.

options.label: constructing an equilateral triangle
options.feedback: That construction builds three 60° angles from equal radii. A perpendicular makes 90°, by halving a straight angle.

options.label: finding a midpoint only
options.feedback: The midpoint of AB is just step one. The right angle needs the second pair of arcs — the bisection of the straight angle.

cp-perp-at-point__mcq.prompt: You raise a perpendicular to line ℓ at point P, and another perpendicular to ℓ at a different point R. How are the two perpendiculars related?

options.label: They are parallel to each other
options.feedback: Both stand at 90° to the same line ℓ, so they point the same way — in a plane, that makes them parallel.

options.label: They intersect at one point above ℓ
options.feedback: Two lines equally perpendicular to ℓ never tilt toward each other — no meeting point. They stay parallel.

options.label: They are perpendicular to each other
options.feedback: Each is perpendicular to ℓ, not to the other. Sharing a perpendicular direction makes them PARALLEL, not mutually perpendicular.

options.label: It depends on how far apart P and R are
options.feedback: Distance doesn't tilt them — both are locked at 90° to ℓ regardless of spacing, so they're always parallel.

cp-perp-at-point__numeric.prompt: The perpendicular at P splits the straight line into two equal angles. How many degrees is each?

commonErrors.feedback: 180° is the WHOLE straight angle. The perpendicular cuts it into two equal pieces: 180 ÷ 2 = 90°.
45° would be a quarter of the straight angle — but a perpendicular makes HALVES: 180 ÷ 2 = 90°.

cp-perp-bisector__mcq.prompt: Why must the compass be opened WIDER than half of AB?

options.label: Otherwise the two arcs are too short to cross
options.feedback: Below half, the arcs can't reach the middle to meet — no crossing points, no bisector line.

options.label: Otherwise the bisector wouldn't be perpendicular
options.feedback: Any equal-radius pair gives a PERPENDICULAR result — the width only controls whether the arcs meet at all.

options.label: So the midpoint lands exactly at the center
options.feedback: The midpoint is determined by AB, not the compass width — width just needs to be big enough for arcs to cross.

options.label: To make the two arcs different sizes
options.feedback: The arcs must be the SAME size (same radius). Width only needs to exceed half so they reach each other.

cp-perp-bisector__mcq.prompt: What property of X and Y proves line XY is the perpendicular bisector of AB?

options.label: Each of X and Y is equidistant from A and B
options.feedback: Same radius from A and from B gives XA = XB and YA = YB — and equidistant points lie on the perpendicular bisector.

options.label: X and Y are the midpoints of the two arcs
options.feedback: Arc midpoints aren't what's used — it's that X and Y sit at EQUAL distances from A and B.

options.label: X and Y are each twice as far from A as from B
options.feedback: The radii are EQUAL, not doubled — XA = XB exactly, which is what puts them on the bisector.

options.label: XY is parallel to AB
options.feedback: XY is PERPENDICULAR to AB, not parallel — it crosses AB at the midpoint at 90°.

cp-perp-bisector__mcq.prompt: You need to construct the MIDPOINT of a segment — no perpendicular required. Which construction gives it to you?

options.label: the perpendicular bisector — its crossing with the segment IS the midpoint
options.feedback: Even when you only want the midpoint, the perpendicular bisector delivers it where it meets the segment.

options.label: copying the segment onto a new ray
options.feedback: Copying reproduces the length elsewhere but never marks the middle of the original.

options.label: drawing a single arc from one endpoint
options.feedback: One arc gives points at a fixed distance from ONE endpoint — not the balanced middle. You need arcs from both.

options.label: connecting the endpoints with a straightedge
options.feedback: That just redraws the segment itself — it marks no interior point.

cp-perp-from-point__mcq.prompt: Line PE is perpendicular to the original line because…

options.label: P and E are both equidistant from C and D, so PE is the perpendicular bisector of CD
options.feedback: PC = PD from the first arc, EC = ED from the last — two equidistant points determine CD's perpendicular bisector, which meets CD at 90°.

options.label: P was directly above the midpoint of CD to begin with
options.feedback: P can sit anywhere above the line — the FIRST arc makes PC = PD automatically, which is what places P on the bisector.

options.label: E is the reflection of P over the line
options.feedback: E does end up as P's mirror image, but that's a CONSEQUENCE of the equidistance construction, not the reason the angle is 90°.

options.label: any line from P to the line is perpendicular
options.feedback: Most lines from P hit at a slant. Only the perpendicular-bisector-of-CD line squares the corner — that's the one PE traces.

cp-perp-from-point__mcq.prompt: Among all segments from P down to the line, which is the shortest?

options.label: the perpendicular one
options.feedback: Every other segment is a hypotenuse whose leg is the perpendicular — and the hypotenuse always exceeds the leg.

options.label: the one reaching the line's left end
options.feedback: Reaching a far point only lengthens the slant. Shortest is straight down — the perpendicular.

options.label: they are all the same length
options.feedback: Slanted paths are strictly longer: each is a hypotenuse over the perpendicular leg. Only the perpendicular is minimal.

options.label: the one making a 45° angle with the line
options.feedback: A 45° segment is still slanted — a hypotenuse, longer than the perpendicular leg beneath it.

cp-perp-from-point__numeric.prompt: Place the line on the x-axis and P at (0, 4). The perpendicular dropped from P meets the line at its foot. What is the x-coordinate of the foot?

commonErrors.feedback: 4 is P's y-coordinate — its HEIGHT above the line, not the foot's position. The foot sits straight below P at x = 0.
3 is where the first ARC crosses the line, not the foot. The perpendicular lands directly under P: x = 0.

cp-perp-from-point__numeric.fallbackFeedback: The foot is directly below P: same x-coordinate, x = 0.

cp-proving-transversal__mcq.prompt: The alternate-interior proof has ∠1 = ∠2 and ∠2 = ∠3. What property gives ∠1 = ∠3?

options.label: Transitive Property
options.feedback: Two equalities sharing ∠2 chain to link ∠1 and ∠3 — transitivity.

options.label: Reflexive Property
options.feedback: Reflexive is self-equality (∠1 = ∠1). Chaining THROUGH ∠2 to a new equality is transitive.

options.label: Corresponding Angles Postulate
options.feedback: That gave the FIRST line (∠1 = ∠2). Combining it with ∠2 = ∠3 is the transitive step.

options.label: Linear Pair Postulate
options.feedback: There's no straight-line sum here — just two equalities chaining, which is transitivity.

cp-proving-transversal__mcq.prompt: A transversal proof needs to conclude two angles are SUPPLEMENTARY (sum 180°). Which fact does it most naturally use?

options.label: a linear pair (two angles on a straight line)
options.feedback: Linear pairs are the source of 180° sums — the go-to for supplementary conclusions.

options.label: vertical angles are equal
options.feedback: Vertical angles give EQUALITY, not a sum. Supplementary conclusions come from linear pairs.

options.label: the reflexive property
options.feedback: Reflexive gives self-equality — useful for shared sides, not for producing a 180° sum.

options.label: the definition of midpoint
options.feedback: Midpoints concern segments, not the angle sums a transversal proof needs. Use a linear pair.

cp-proving-transversal__numeric.prompt: Across two parallel lines, alternate interior angles measure (2x + 15)° and (4x − 25)°. Find the measure of either angle, in degrees.

commonErrors.feedback: 20 is the value of X, not the angle. Substitute back: 2(20) + 15 = 55°.
125° treats the pair as CO-INTERIOR (supplementary): 180 − 55. But alternate interior angles are EQUAL — set 2x+15 = 4x−25, giving the angle 55°.

cp-square-triangle__mcq.prompt: Which inscribed polygon is built from two PERPENDICULAR diameters?

options.label: the square
options.feedback: Perpendicular diameters cross the circle at four points 90° apart — the square's vertices.

options.label: the hexagon
options.feedback: The hexagon comes from stepping the RADIUS around (60° arcs), not from perpendicular diameters.

options.label: the equilateral triangle
options.feedback: The triangle uses every other hexagon mark (120° arcs) — no perpendicular diameter is needed.

options.label: the regular pentagon
options.feedback: The pentagon needs 72° arcs, which neither radius-stepping nor perpendicular diameters produce directly.

cp-square-triangle__numeric.prompt: An inscribed square's four vertices divide the circle equally. What is each central angle, in degrees?

commonErrors.feedback: 360° is the WHOLE turn. Split it among the four vertices: 360 ÷ 4 = 90°.
45° would be 360 ÷ 8 — an octagon's spacing. A square has 4 vertices: 360 ÷ 4 = 90°.

cp-square-triangle__numeric.prompt: Using the radius-stepping method, the compass makes 6 equally spaced marks. How many of them are the vertices of the inscribed equilateral TRIANGLE?

commonErrors.feedback: 6 marks make the HEXAGON. The triangle keeps every OTHER one: 3 vertices.
4 vertices make a square — and the square comes from perpendicular diameters, not the 6 radius-marks. The triangle uses 3 of the 6.

cp-square-triangle__numeric.fallbackFeedback: Every other of the 6 marks: 3 vertices.

cp-tool-rules__mcq.prompt: Why do classical constructions forbid using the ruler's measurement marks?

options.label: So the result is provably exact, not just measured close
options.feedback: Equal radii and straight lines give EXACT relationships you can prove — measurement only ever approximates.

options.label: Because rulers are less accurate than compasses
options.feedback: It's not about tool accuracy — even a perfect ruler is banned. The point is provable exactness from geometry alone.

options.label: Because ancient Greeks had no rulers
options.feedback: They had marked measuring tools; the restriction is a deliberate mathematical choice, not a shortage.

options.label: To make the constructions harder for practice
options.feedback: The restriction isn't busywork — it guarantees every constructed length rests on a proof, not a reading.

cp-transversal-family__numeric.prompt: A transversal crosses two parallel lines; one angle is 70°. Its CORRESPONDING angle measures how many degrees?

commonErrors.feedback: 110° = 180 − 70 is the SUPPLEMENT — that's a same-side or linear-pair relationship. Corresponding angles are EQUAL: 70°.
20° = 90 − 70 is a complement, not a transversal relationship. Corresponding angles are equal: 70°.

cp-transversal-family__numeric.prompt: Across the same parallels, the CO-INTERIOR (same-side interior) partner of a 55° angle measures how many degrees?

commonErrors.feedback: 55° would make them EQUAL — that's the ALTERNATE interior relationship. Same-side interior angles are SUPPLEMENTARY: 180 − 55 = 125°.
305° = 360 − 55 uses a full turn. Co-interior angles fill a straight angle: 180 − 55 = 125°.

cp-transversal-family__numeric.prompt: A transversal crosses two parallel lines. One interior angle is 112°. What is its CO-INTERIOR (same-side interior) partner, in degrees?

commonErrors.feedback: 112° is the ALTERNATE interior partner (opposite side, equal). The SAME-side partner is supplementary: 180 − 112 = 68°.
248° = 360 − 112 uses a full turn. Co-interior angles fill a straight angle: 180 − 112 = 68°.

cp-two-column__mcq.prompt: What must the FIRST statement of a two-column proof be based on?

options.label: the given information
options.feedback: You start from what the problem hands you — the given — and reason forward from there.

options.label: the thing you are trying to prove
options.feedback: Starting from the conclusion assumes what you must earn — that's circular. Begin with the given instead.

options.label: any true fact you happen to know
options.feedback: Only facts RELEVANT and licensed by this problem belong — you launch from the given, not from trivia.

options.label: a guess to be checked later
options.feedback: Proofs never rest on guesses. The first line is solid: the given information.

cp-two-column__mcq.prompt: In a proof, two triangles share side XY, and the proof writes "XY = XY." What is the reason?

options.label: Reflexive Property
options.feedback: Anything equals itself; a shared side is justified by the Reflexive Property.

options.label: Given
options.feedback: The shared side usually isn't stated in the setup — it's SEEN in the figure and justified as self-equal: Reflexive.

options.label: Symmetric Property
options.feedback: Symmetric flips an equality between two DIFFERENT things. XY = XY is one thing equal to itself — Reflexive.

options.label: Definition of congruence
options.feedback: That definition links congruent figures to equal parts. A side equal to ITSELF is simply Reflexive.

cp-two-column__mcq.prompt: Which of these makes a two-column-proof line INVALID?

options.label: Its reason cites a statement that appears later in the proof
options.feedback: Reasons must point backward only — using a not-yet-established line is circular and illegal.

options.label: Its reason is 'Given'
options.feedback: "Given" is a perfectly valid reason — it cites the problem's setup, the legitimate starting point.

options.label: Its reason is a definition
options.feedback: Definitions are core, legal reasons — they license statements throughout a proof.

options.label: Its statement repeats a value equal to itself
options.feedback: A self-equal statement (Reflexive) is legal and often useful — not a flaw at all.

cp-vertical-angles__mcq.prompt: Why does a linear pair of angles always sum to 180°?

options.label: Together they form a straight angle, which is 180°
options.feedback: The two angles fill a straight line exactly — a straight angle — so their measures total 180°.

options.label: Because all angles sum to 180°
options.feedback: Only pairs forming a straight line sum to 180° — not every angle pair does. A linear pair is exactly the straight-line case.

options.label: Because the two angles are always equal
options.feedback: A linear pair is equal only when both are 90°. In general they're unequal but still SUM to 180°.

options.label: Because vertical angles are equal
options.feedback: That's the theorem we're trying to PROVE — a linear pair's 180° comes from the straight angle, and is what we'll USE to prove it.

cp-vertical-angles__mcq.prompt: In the vertical-angles proof, what single move turns the two linear-pair equations into ∠1 = ∠3?

options.label: Subtracting the shared angle ∠2 from both equal sums
options.feedback: Both sums equal 180° (hence each other); removing the common ∠2 leaves ∠1 = ∠3.

options.label: Measuring ∠1 and ∠3 with a protractor
options.feedback: Measuring gives one example, not a proof. The algebra of subtracting ∠2 settles all cases at once.

options.label: Assuming ∠1 = ∠3 to begin with
options.feedback: Assuming the conclusion is circular. The proof DERIVES it by cancelling ∠2, never assumes it.

options.label: Adding the two equations together
options.feedback: Adding gives ∠1 + 2∠2 + ∠3 = 360 — a tangle. SUBTRACTING the shared ∠2 is the clean move.

cp-vertical-angles__numeric.prompt: Two lines cross. One angle measures (3x + 10)°; its VERTICAL angle measures (5x − 30)°. Solve for x.

commonErrors.feedback: x = 25 comes from treating them as a LINEAR pair: (3x+10)+(5x−30)=180. But VERTICAL angles are EQUAL, so set 3x+10 = 5x−30 → x = 20.
x = 10 solves 3x + 10 = 5x − 30 only if you slip a sign — recheck: 10 + 30 = 5x − 3x gives 40 = 2x, so x = 20.

cp-vertical-angles__numeric.prompt: Two lines cross. One angle is (4x)° and the angle NEXT to it (a linear pair) is (2x + 30)°. Find the measure of the angle VERTICAL to the (4x)° angle, in degrees.

commonErrors.feedback: 80° is the (2x + 30) angle at x = 25 — the LINEAR-pair neighbor. The angle VERTICAL to 4x equals 4x itself: 4(25) = 100°.
25 is the value of x, not an angle. Substitute: the 4x angle is 100°, and its vertical angle equals it: 100°.

cp-vertical-angles__numeric.fallbackFeedback: Linear pair: 6x + 30 = 180 → x = 25; the 4x angle is 100°, and its vertical angle equals it: 100°.

cp-why-works__mcq.prompt: The perpendicular-bisector proof concludes the two triangles are congruent by which criterion?

options.label: SSS (three pairs of equal sides)
options.feedback: XA = XB, YA = YB, and the shared side XY — three equal sides, so SSS.

options.label: SAS (two sides and the included angle)
options.feedback: The compass gives only equal LENGTHS, never a known equal angle — so with three equal sides the criterion is SSS.

options.label: AAA (three equal angles)
options.feedback: AAA isn't even a congruence criterion (it gives similarity), and no angles are measured here. Use the equal sides: SSS.

options.label: HL (hypotenuse-leg)
options.feedback: HL needs a known right angle FIRST — but the right angle is what we're trying to PROVE. The proof gets there via SSS.

cp-why-works__mcq.prompt: Once a construction proof shows two triangles are congruent, what can it conclude?

options.label: every pair of corresponding sides and angles is equal
options.feedback: Congruent triangles match in ALL parts — the proof then reads off whichever equal angle or side it needs.

options.label: only that the triangles have the same area
options.feedback: Equal area is a weak by-product — congruence gives far more: every corresponding side AND angle matches.

options.label: only that the triangles look similar
options.feedback: Congruence is stronger than similarity: not just equal angles but equal SIZES too, part for part.

options.label: nothing further without measuring
options.feedback: Congruence itself delivers all corresponding parts equal — no measuring needed, that's the point.

cp-why-works__mcq.prompt: Why isn't a very carefully measured drawing enough to PROVE a construction works?

options.label: A drawing can be slightly off in ways too small to see; only a logical chain from guaranteed facts is certain
options.feedback: Measurement has limits and hands shake — a proof from equal radii through SSS is exact and covers every case.

options.label: Drawings are always completely wrong
options.feedback: Good drawings are close and useful as evidence — the issue is they can't GUARANTEE exactness, not that they're worthless.

options.label: Proofs are just a formality once you've measured
options.feedback: The proof is what upgrades "looks right in this case" to "is right in every case" — not a formality but the actual guarantee.

options.label: You'd need to measure in more than one place
options.feedback: Even infinitely many measurements are still measurements, each with error. A proof needs zero measurements — just valid reasoning.

cx-circle-position__mcq.prompt: A delivery zone centered at (4, 3) is drawn just large enough to include the house at (10, 11). Is the warehouse at (0, 0) inside the zone?

options.label: Yes — the zone's r² = 100, and the origin evaluates to only 25: deep inside

options.label: Every point at distance exactly 5 from O
options.feedback: The definition is a distance test: pass at exactly 5, you're on the circle; anything else, you're not.

options.label: Every point at distance 5 or less from O
options.feedback: Distance ≤ 5 describes the filled DISK. The circle is only the boundary — the points at exactly 5.

options.label: Every point inside the round shape, plus O
options.feedback: Interior points are closer than 5, so they fail the distance test — and O itself sits at distance 0.

options.label: The points where the circle crosses a line through O
options.feedback: That's just two points of it. The circle is ALL points at distance 5 — infinitely many, all the way around.

gf-find-motion__mcq.prompt: A(1, 4) and B(3, 1) map to A′(−1, −4) and B′(−3, −1). Which motion is it?

options.label: a 180° rotation about the origin
options.feedback: Both signs of both points flipped, order intact — exactly (x, y) → (−x, −y).

options.label: reflection over the y-axis
options.feedback: That mirror flips only x: A would land at (−1, 4), but A′ has y = −4 too.

options.label: reflection over the x-axis
options.feedback: That mirror flips only y: A would land at (1, −4), but A′'s x also flipped to −1.

options.label: reflection over the line y = x
options.feedback: The swap sends A(1,4) to (4,1) — no sign changes at all. These images are fully negated instead.

gf-find-motion__mcq.prompt: A(0, 0), B(5, 0) — so AB = 5. C(2, 1), D(2, 7) — so CD = 6. Is there a rigid motion mapping segment AB onto segment CD?

options.label: No — the lengths differ (5 vs 6), and rigid motions preserve length
options.feedback: One mismatched distance is a complete proof of impossibility: rigid motions never stretch.

options.label: Yes — translate A to C, then rotate B around to D
options.feedback: The rotation swings B on a radius-5 circle around C — and D sits 6 away, off that circle. The endpoint can never land.

options.label: Yes — a 90° rotation turns horizontal segments into vertical ones
options.feedback: It fixes the DIRECTION mismatch but not the length: the rotated segment is still 5 long, one unit short of CD.

options.label: It cannot be decided from coordinates alone
options.feedback: Coordinates decide it completely — they give exact lengths (5 and 6), and unequal lengths forbid any rigid motion.

gf-find-motion__numeric.prompt: Using the translation (x, y) → (x + 2, y + 4) from the last problem: point (2, 2) lies inside ΔABC. What is the x-coordinate of its image?

commonErrors.feedback: 6 is 2 + 4 — the y-shift applied to x. Keep each shift in its own slot: x gets +2, so 2 + 2 = 4.
2 is unmoved — but the motion carries EVERY point of the figure, interior included: 2 + 2 = 4.

gf-line-symmetry__mcq.prompt: Which shape has EXACTLY 4 lines of symmetry?

options.label: a square
options.feedback: Two midlines plus two diagonals = 4 — the regular 4-gon gets its full n lines.

options.label: a (non-square) rectangle
options.feedback: The rectangle stops at 2 — its diagonal folds land long sides on short sides and fail.

options.label: a regular hexagon
options.feedback: Regular n-gon means n lines: the hexagon has 6, one more pair than asked for.

options.label: a parallelogram (no right angles)
options.feedback: A generic parallelogram has ZERO lines — every candidate fold mismatches the slanted sides. (Its symmetry is a different kind — next lesson.)

gf-line-symmetry__numeric.prompt: How many lines of symmetry does a (non-square) rectangle have?

commonErrors.feedback: 4 counts the diagonals — but fold a rectangle along a diagonal and the long side lands on a SHORT side. Diagonal mirrors belong to the square; the rectangle keeps only its 2 midlines.
There are two midline folds, not one: top-onto-bottom AND left-onto-right both match perfectly.

gf-line-symmetry__numeric.fallbackFeedback: The two midlines — vertical and horizontal — and nothing else: 2.

gf-line-symmetry__numeric.prompt: How many lines of symmetry does a REGULAR pentagon have?

commonErrors.feedback: 1 is just the vertical fold — but the pentagon is regular, so every vertex-to-opposite-edge fold works the same way. Five vertices, five lines.
10 double-counts: a fold through a vertex and the opposite edge midpoint is ONE line, not two. Regular n-gon: exactly n lines — here 5.

gf-notation__mcq.prompt: Which of these is guaranteed to name the SAME object as line PQ?

options.label: line QP
options.feedback: A line runs forever both ways — either point can be listed first.

options.label: ray PQ
options.feedback: A ray starts at P and runs one way only. Line PQ has no starting point — it runs both ways.

options.label: segment PQ
options.feedback: Segment PQ stops at both P and Q. The line continues forever past each of them.

options.label: ray QP
options.feedback: Ray QP starts at Q and runs one way. The line through P and Q has no endpoint at all.

gf-notation__mcq.prompt: Which angle name has its vertex at T?

options.label: ∠STU
options.feedback: Middle letter T = vertex T. The rays run from T through S and through U.

options.label: ∠TSU
options.feedback: Here the middle letter is S — this angle's vertex is S, with T just a point on one ray.

options.label: ∠SUT
options.feedback: Middle letter U puts the vertex at U. T rides along a ray instead of sitting at the corner.

options.label: ∠UST
options.feedback: The middle letter is S again — same vertex-S angle as ∠TSU, just read from the other side.

gf-notation__mcq.prompt: ∠ABD has vertex B; point C lies on ray BD beyond D. Which is a VALID alternate name for ∠ABD?

options.label: ∠ABC
options.feedback: C rides the same ray as D (ray BD extended through C is still ray BC = ray BD), so ∠ABC names the very same opening at vertex B.

options.label: ∠BAD
options.feedback: The middle letter here is A — that names an angle with vertex A, a different corner altogether.

options.label: ∠ADB
options.feedback: Middle letter D puts the vertex at D. Same three letters, wrong one in the middle.

options.label: ∠DBC
options.feedback: D and C sit on the SAME ray from B, so these two "sides" collapse into one ray — no opening, no angle.

gf-notation__mcq.prompt: Segments AB and CD match exactly. Which statement is written correctly?

options.label: AB = CD (comparing the lengths)
options.feedback: Plain AB and CD are numbers — the lengths — and numbers compare with =.

options.label: AB ≅ CD (comparing the lengths)
options.feedback: Plain AB is already a number, and numbers take =. The ≅ symbol is reserved for the figures themselves.

options.label: m(segment AB) ≅ m(segment CD)
options.feedback: Measures are numbers, and numbers take = — the m(…) wrapper makes ≅ doubly out of place.

options.label: AB = segment CD
options.feedback: This equates a number with a figure — a type mismatch no matter which symbol sits between them.

gf-notation__mcq.prompt: An angle at vertex A measures 40 degrees. Which statement records that correctly?

options.label: m∠A = 40°
options.feedback: m∠A is a number and 40° is a number — a legal = pairing.

options.label: ∠A = 40°
options.feedback: ∠A is the figure itself — a figure can't equal a number. The measure m∠A is what equals 40°.

options.label: ∠A ≅ 40°
options.feedback: ≅ joins two FIGURES, and 40° is a number — this mixes types in a new way.

options.label: m∠A ≅ 40°
options.feedback: Both sides are numbers here, so the symbol must be =, not the figure-symbol ≅.

gf-notation__mcq.prompt: Which notebook line is correctly written?

options.label: XY = 7
options.feedback: XY without a hat is the LENGTH — a number — and 7 is a number. Numbers pair with =.

options.label: ∠D = ∠E
options.feedback: ∠D and ∠E are figures — they'd need ≅. (Their MEASURES, m∠D and m∠E, are what take =.)

options.label: m∠D ≅ 40°
options.feedback: m∠D and 40° are both numbers — the pairing must be m∠D = 40°.

options.label: segment XY ≅ 7
options.feedback: A segment is a figure and 7 is a number — no symbol can legally join those two types.

gf-reflection-rule__mcq.prompt: P′ is the reflection of P over line m (and P is not on m). What is the exact relationship between m and segment PP′?

options.label: m is the perpendicular bisector of PP′
options.feedback: The full mirror property: PP′ meets m at a right angle, and m cuts PP′ into congruent halves.

options.label: m is parallel to PP′
options.feedback: Parallel would mean PP′ never crosses the mirror — but a point and its image sit on OPPOSITE sides, so the segment must cross it.

options.label: m bisects PP′ but at any convenient angle
options.feedback: Equal halves alone isn't enough — a slanted crossing would smear the reflection. The crossing must be at 90°.

options.label: m passes through P′ only
options.feedback: P′ sits OFF the mirror, exactly as far from it as P — the line passes through the segment's MIDPOINT instead.

gf-reflection-rule__mcq.prompt: The point (4, 4) lies ON the line y = x. Where does the reflection over y = x send it?

options.label: Nowhere new — it is its own image (a fixed point)
options.feedback: The swap returns (4, 4) unchanged. Every point of the mirror line stays put — that's what makes it the mirror.

options.label: To (−4, −4), the opposite side of the origin
options.feedback: Both signs flipping is the 180° rotation's signature. Reflection over y = x only SWAPS — and swapping equal coordinates changes nothing.

options.label: Reflection is undefined for points on the line
options.feedback: The rule handles it fine: (4, 4) → (4, 4). Being on the mirror just means the point maps to itself.

options.label: It slides along the line to (5, 5)
options.feedback: Sliding along a line is a TRANSLATION. Reflections move points straight ACROSS the mirror — and zero distance across is no move at all.

gf-reflection-rule__numeric.prompt: Reflect (−4, 6) over the y-axis. What is the image's x-coordinate?

commonErrors.feedback: −4 is the preimage's x, unflipped — that would happen under an X-AXIS reflection. Over the y-axis, x changes sign: +4.
6 is the y-coordinate, which the y-axis reflection leaves alone. The question asks for the flipped x: 4.

gf-reflection-rule__numeric.prompt: Reflect (7, 3) over the line y = x. What is the image's x-coordinate?

commonErrors.feedback: 7 stayed in the x-slot — but this mirror SWAPS the slots: the new x is the old y, 3.
Sign flips belong to the AXIS mirrors — the y = x mirror never negates. Here the coordinates just trade places: new x = 3.

gf-rotation-rule__mcq.prompt: Apply a 90° counterclockwise rotation to (5, 2), then apply it AGAIN to the result. Where does the point end up?

options.feedback: Twice through (−y, x): (5, 2) → (−2, 5) → (−5, −2) — exactly the 180° rule, since 90 + 90 = 180.
(−2, 5) is the point after ONE quarter turn. The second application still has to run: (−2, 5) → (−5, −2).
Returning home takes a FULL turn (360°) — two quarters only make a half. (Two identical REFLECTIONS cancel; rotations keep adding.)
(2, −5) is the 270° result — a quarter turn the CLOCKWISE way. Two CCW quarters add to 180°: (−5, −2).

gf-rotation-rule__numeric.prompt: Rotate (4, 1) by 90° counterclockwise about the origin. What is the image's y-coordinate?

commonErrors.feedback: 1 is the preimage's y riding along unchanged — but a quarter turn moves it into the x-slot. The NEW y is the old x: 4.
−4 is the 270° (clockwise-quarter) result, (y, −x). Counterclockwise 90° puts +x into the y-slot: 4.

gf-rotation-rule__numeric.fallbackFeedback: 90° CCW rule (−y, x): new y = old x = 4.

gf-rotation-rule__numeric.prompt: Rotate (1, 7) by 270° counterclockwise about the origin. What is the image's y-coordinate?

commonErrors.feedback: 1 is the old x WITHOUT its sign flip. The 270° rule is (y, −x) — the x moves to the y-slot negated: −1.
7 is the old y — under this turn it moves to the X-slot. The new y is −x = −1.

gf-rotational-symmetry__mcq.prompt: Which letter has rotational symmetry of order 2 (matches itself after a 180° turn)?

options.label: N
options.feedback: Upside-down N is still N — the two verticals trade places and the diagonal maps onto itself: order 2.

options.label: A
options.feedback: Half-turned, A stands on its point — the letter no longer reads as itself. A's symmetry is a MIRROR (vertical line), not a turn.

options.label: E
options.feedback: A 180° turn sends E's three arms pointing LEFT — clearly not an E. Its real symmetry is the horizontal MIRROR (top folds onto bottom), which is a reflection, not a rotation.

options.label: T
options.feedback: Half-turned T stands on its crossbar — upside down. T's symmetry is the vertical mirror line only.

gf-rotational-symmetry__mcq.prompt: Which shape has ROTATIONAL symmetry but NO line symmetry?

options.label: a parallelogram (no right angles, unequal sides)
options.feedback: It matches itself at 180° — yet no fold works: the slanted sides always land wrong. Rotation-only, the sneaky cell.

options.label: a square
options.feedback: The square has BOTH: order-4 rotation and 4 mirror lines — too symmetric for this cell.

options.label: an isosceles triangle (not equilateral)
options.feedback: The opposite cell: one mirror line down the middle, but no rotation under 360° matches — mirror-only.

options.label: a scalene triangle
options.feedback: Neither kind: no fold matches unequal sides, and no partial turn does either.

gf-rotational-symmetry__numeric.prompt: A regular hexagon has rotational symmetry of order 6. What is its SMALLEST matching rotation, in degrees?

commonErrors.feedback: 6 is the ORDER — the count of matching positions. The angle divides the turn among them: 360 ÷ 6 = 60°.
120° is 360 ÷ 3 — an order-3 answer (the triangle's). With SIX positions the step shrinks to 60°.

gf-translation-rule__mcq.prompt: A translation sends A(3, 5) to A′(8, 2). What is the rule?

options.label: (x, y) → (x + 5, y − 3)
options.feedback: 8 − 3 = +5 right, 2 − 5 = −3 down — and plugging A back in lands exactly on A′.

options.label: (x, y) → (x − 5, y + 3)
options.feedback: That's the rule from A′ BACK to A — preimage minus image. Compute image − preimage instead: +5 and −3.

options.label: (x, y) → (x + 8, y + 2)
options.feedback: 8 and 2 are A′'s COORDINATES, not the shifts. The shift is how far the point MOVED: image minus preimage.

options.label: (x, y) → (x + 5, y + 3)
options.feedback: The x-shift is right, but the y fell from 5 to 2 — a NEGATIVE shift: y − 3, not y + 3.

gf-translation-rule__numeric.prompt: The translation (x, y) → (x − 4, y + 7) sends (10, 2) to (a, 9). Find a.

commonErrors.feedback: 14 is 10 + 4 — the minus sign flipped. x − 4 slides LEFT: 10 − 4 = 6.
10 is the preimage x, unchanged — but the rule's first slot says every x moves by −4: 10 − 4 = 6.

gf-translation-rule__numeric.prompt: Start at (6, 9). Apply (x, y) → (x + 2, y − 5), THEN (x, y) → (x − 7, y + 1). What is the x-coordinate of the final image?

commonErrors.feedback: 15 is 6 + 2 + 7 — the −7 turned positive. The second slide goes LEFT: 8 − 7 = 1.
8 is where x sits after the FIRST slide only. The second rule still has to act: 8 − 7 = 1.

gf-undefined-terms__mcq.prompt: Why does geometry leave point, line, and plane UNDEFINED?

options.label: Nobody has found good definitions for them yet
options.feedback: It's not a gap waiting to be filled — it's a deliberate choice. Definitions need earlier words, so SOME terms must be the agreed starting stock.

options.label: Every definition uses earlier terms, so some terms must come first, undefined
options.feedback: Exactly — they're the floor the whole tower of definitions stands on.

options.label: They are too simple to matter in proofs
options.feedback: They matter enormously — nearly every later definition (segment, angle, circle) is built directly from them.

options.label: They can only be understood with coordinates
options.feedback: Coordinates come later and are optional — the undefined terms are the coordinate-free starting point.

gf-undefined-terms__mcq.prompt: Suppose someone claims TWO different lines both pass through points X and Y. Which postulate does the claim break?

options.label: Through any two distinct points there is exactly one line
options.feedback: The claim gives two lines through the same pair — uniqueness says at most one, so the "two" lines must really be the same line.

options.label: A line extends forever in both directions
options.feedback: Both claimed lines could extend forever and the claim would still be broken — endlessness isn't the issue; UNIQUENESS is.

options.label: Two points determine a segment
options.feedback: True but beside the point: segments are about endpoints, and the claim is about how many LINES fit through the pair.

options.label: A plane contains at least three points
options.feedback: That postulate is about planes having enough room — it says nothing about how many lines fit through two points.

pq-capstone__mcq.prompt: A figure shows tick marks: the two TOP sides match each other, the two BOTTOM sides match each other (top ≠ bottom). No other marks. Most specific name?

options.label: Kite — two pairs of congruent CONSECUTIVE sides
options.feedback: Each pair shares a vertex (top pair at the apex, bottom pair at the tail) — the kite's defining geography.

options.label: Parallelogram — two pairs of congruent sides
options.feedback: The parallelogram test needs OPPOSITE pairs; these pairs are consecutive. That's kite country.

options.label: Isosceles trapezoid
options.feedback: That needs a marked PARALLEL pair with congruent legs — no parallel marks appear here. The consecutive ticks say kite.

options.label: Rhombus — sides congruent in pairs
options.feedback: A rhombus needs all FOUR sides equal; here top ≠ bottom. Two distinct consecutive pairs: kite.

pq-capstone__numeric.prompt: A quadrilateral's diagonals (10 and 24) bisect each other at right angles. Find its side length.

commonErrors.feedback: 17 = 5 + 12 adds the half-diagonals — they're perpendicular LEGS: √(5² + 12²) = 13.
26 = √(10² + 24²) forgot to halve the diagonals first: √(5² + 12²) = 13.
34 = 10 + 24 adds full diagonals — neither halved nor Pythagorized: 13.
13 is ONE side — the rhombus has four of them: 52.
120 = ½ × 10 × 24 is the AREA (the perpendicular-diagonals formula) — the perimeter adds sides: 52.
68 = 2 × (10 + 24) treats the diagonals as sides — sides are 13 each: 52.

pq-capstone__numeric.prompt: A quadrilateral's diagonals bisect each other AND are congruent, each measuring 17. One side is 8. Find the adjacent side.

commonErrors.feedback: 9 = 17 − 8 subtracts lengths — Pythagoras subtracts SQUARES: √(289 − 64) = 15.
18.79 ≈ √(289 + 64) ADDS — but 17 is the hypotenuse (the diagonal), so subtract: 15.
12.5 = (17 + 8)/2 averages — the certified rectangle calls for the right-triangle relationship: 15.

pq-exterior-sum__numeric.prompt: Four exterior angles of a pentagon are 85°, 60°, 70°, and 75°. The fifth?

commonErrors.feedback: 250 = 540 − 290 reaches for the INTERIOR sum. Exterior angles close a 360° lap: 360 − 290 = 70°.
290 is the four turns so far — the fifth finishes the lap: 360 − 290 = 70°.

pq-hierarchy__mcq.prompt: “A rectangle is a parallelogram.” Always, sometimes, or never?

options.label: Always — rectangle is DEFINED as a special parallelogram
options.feedback: Membership flows up: every rectangle carries the parallelogram definition inside its own.

options.label: Sometimes — only when the sides differ
options.feedback: Side lengths never matter for this one — the parallelogram requirement is built into being a rectangle. Always.

options.label: Never — they're different shapes
options.feedback: Different NAMES, nested sets: the rectangle region lives wholly inside the parallelogram region.

options.label: Sometimes — only when it's also a square
options.feedback: Squarehood is irrelevant here; even the most elongated rectangle is a parallelogram. Always.

pq-hierarchy__mcq.prompt: “A parallelogram is a rectangle.” Always, sometimes, or never?

options.label: Sometimes — exactly when it has a right angle
options.feedback: Downward claims are conditional: the leaning ones fail, the right-angled ones qualify.

options.label: Always — the terms coincide
options.feedback: A 60°-leaning parallelogram is the counterexample — no right angles, no rectangle. Sometimes.

options.label: Never — parallelograms exclude rectangles
options.feedback: Rectangles are IN the parallelogram family — the claim succeeds precisely on those members. Sometimes.

options.label: Sometimes — exactly when all sides are congruent
options.feedback: All-congruent-sides makes a RHOMBUS. The rectangle condition is the right ANGLE. Sometimes, but for the angle reason.

pq-hierarchy__mcq.prompt: Under this course's convention, “a parallelogram is a trapezoid” is:

options.label: Never true — exactly one parallel pair excludes two-pair figures
options.feedback: The exclusive definition splits the branches cleanly: two parallel pairs means not-a-trapezoid, full stop.

options.label: Always true — it has at least one parallel pair
options.feedback: That's the OTHER convention (“at least one”). Ours says exactly one, so parallelograms are excluded.

options.label: Sometimes true — when it leans
options.feedback: Leaning never removes the second parallel pair — every parallelogram keeps both pairs at any slant. Never.

options.label: Sometimes true — when it's a rhombus
options.feedback: A rhombus has two parallel pairs like every parallelogram — still excluded under exactly-one. Never.

pq-hierarchy__mcq.prompt: Verdicts for: (A) a square is a rectangle; (B) a rectangle is a square; (C) a rhombus is a trapezoid.

options.label: A: always. B: sometimes. C: never
options.feedback: Up-flow, down-flow, branch-jump — the three logical directions of the family tree, one of each.

options.label: A: sometimes. B: sometimes. C: sometimes
options.feedback: Only B is conditional. A holds by definition (up-flow); C is blocked by the exactly-one-pair convention.

options.label: A: always. B: never. C: never
options.feedback: B isn't never — rectangles with congruent consecutive sides ARE squares. Down-flow means sometimes.

options.label: A: always. B: sometimes. C: always
options.feedback: C fails our convention: a rhombus's TWO parallel pairs exceed the trapezoid's exactly-one. Never.

pq-interior-sum__numeric.prompt: Four angles of a pentagon are 100°, 110°, 95°, and 120°. Find the fifth.

commonErrors.feedback: 295 = 720 − 425 uses the HEXAGON's sum. Five sides hold (5 − 2) × 180 = 540: the fifth angle is 115°.
425 is the four givens added up — the question wants what's LEFT of 540: 115°.

pq-para-diagonals__mcq.prompt: Which diagonal property holds in EVERY parallelogram?

options.label: They bisect each other
options.feedback: The four-small-triangles ASA argument works in every parallelogram — mutual halving is universal.

options.label: They are equal in length
options.feedback: Equal diagonals is the RECTANGLE's signature — skew a rectangle and one diagonal stretches while the other shrinks.

options.label: They are perpendicular
options.feedback: Perpendicular diagonals mark the RHOMBUS. A long, low parallelogram crosses its diagonals at a shallow angle.

options.label: They bisect the corner angles
options.feedback: Angle-bisecting diagonals also belong to the RHOMBUS. The universal fact is that each diagonal halves the other.

pq-para-diagonals__numeric.prompt: Diagonal AC of a parallelogram measures 18, meeting BD at O. Find AO.

commonErrors.feedback: 18 is the WHOLE diagonal — O sits at its midpoint, so AO is half: 9.
36 doubles it — backwards. From whole to half: 18/2 = 9.

pq-para-diagonals__numeric.prompt: In the same parallelogram, BO = 7. Find the full diagonal BD.

commonErrors.feedback: 7 is only the HALF from B to O — the diagonal continues equally beyond: BD = 14.
28 doubles the whole — BO is a half, so one doubling suffices: 2 × 7 = 14.

pq-para-diagonals__numeric.prompt: With AO = 2x + 3 and OC = x + 8, find the FULL diagonal AC.

commonErrors.feedback: 5 is x — the question asks the diagonal's LENGTH. Each half is 13, so AC = 26.
13 is one HALF (AO). The diagonal spans both halves: 2 × 13 = 26.

pq-para-tests__mcq.prompt: “One pair of opposite sides is parallel, and the OTHER pair is congruent.” Which figure proves this is NOT a valid parallelogram test?

options.label: An isosceles trapezoid
options.feedback: Parallel bases + congruent legs, yet only one parallel pair — the data holds, the conclusion fails. Counterexample complete.

options.label: A square
options.feedback: A square IS a parallelogram — it can't witness the test failing. You need a figure with the data but WITHOUT parallelogram-hood.

options.label: A kite
options.feedback: A typical kite has NO parallel sides, so it doesn't even satisfy the test's data — it can't test the implication.

options.label: There is none — the test is valid
options.feedback: The isosceles trapezoid defeats it: bases parallel, legs congruent, not a parallelogram. Same-pair is what makes test 4 work.

pq-para-tests__mcq.prompt: Which single fact about quadrilateral PQRS certifies it is a parallelogram?

options.label: PQ ≅ SR and PQ ∥ SR (the same pair, both jobs)
options.feedback: Test 4: one pair doing double duty. The diagonal + SAS + CPCTC proof makes the other pair parallel for free.

options.label: PQ ≅ SR and PS ∥ QR (mixed pairs)
options.feedback: Mixed pairs is the isosceles-trapezoid trap — congruent legs with the OTHER pair parallel certifies nothing.

options.label: Diagonal PR bisects diagonal QS (one-way)
options.feedback: One-way bisection is a KITE behavior — the test needs MUTUAL bisection, each diagonal cutting the other in half.

options.label: One pair of congruent angles
options.feedback: The angle test needs BOTH pairs of opposite angles congruent — a single pair leaves the shape loose.

pq-para-tests__mcq.prompt: A builder knows: AB ≅ CD, and AD ∥ BC. Which ONE additional measurement certifies a parallelogram?

options.label: Show AD ≅ BC — then the parallel pair is also congruent (test 4)
options.feedback: Now AD carries both jobs: congruent AND parallel. One clean measurement upgrades the invalid mix into a valid certificate.

options.label: Show AB ∥ AD
options.feedback: AB and AD are CONSECUTIVE sides — in a parallelogram they're never parallel (they meet at a vertex). That would break the shape, not certify it.

options.label: Measure one diagonal's length
options.feedback: A single diagonal length certifies nothing — the diagonal test needs both diagonals CUT AT MIDPOINTS, a different setup.

options.label: No single measurement can ever suffice
options.feedback: One does: AD ≅ BC turns the parallel pair into a congruent-AND-parallel pair — test 4 fires immediately.

pq-para-tests__numeric.prompt: Quadrilateral ABCD has diagonals meeting at O, with AO = x + 4 and OC = 3x − 10. For what value of AO does the diagonal-bisection test apply (given BO = OD already)?

commonErrors.feedback: 7 is x — the test needs the segment length: AO = x + 4 = 11.
22 is the full diagonal AC after the test passes. AO alone is half: 11.
3 solves x + 4 = 3x − … incorrectly — collect terms: 14 = 2x, x = 7, AO = 11.

pq-rectangle__mcq.prompt: In rectangle ABCD with diagonals meeting at O, which statement is true because it's a RECTANGLE (not just a parallelogram)?

options.label: AC = BD
options.feedback: Congruent diagonals are the rectangle's signature — a generic parallelogram's diagonals differ in length.

options.label: AO = OC
options.feedback: That's mutual bisection — every parallelogram does it (ch2). The rectangle's new gift is AC = BD.

options.label: AB = DC
options.feedback: Opposite sides congruent is the ch2 parallelogram property — no right angle needed. The upgrade is AC = BD.

options.label: AB ∥ DC
options.feedback: Parallel opposite sides is the parallelogram DEFINITION itself. The rectangle adds congruent diagonals: AC = BD.

pq-rectangle__mcq.prompt: A carpenter measures a doorframe's two diagonals and finds them equal (the frame's opposite sides are already equal). What's certified?

options.label: The frame is a true rectangle — right angles guaranteed

options.label: the circle passing through all three vertices (the circumscribed circle)
options.feedback: Equal distance to each vertex means one circle, centered there, hits all three — the circumcircle.

options.label: the circle touching all three sides
options.feedback: That inscribed circle is centered at the INCENTER. The circumcenter's circle passes through the VERTICES.

options.label: the largest circle that fits inside
options.feedback: The largest inscribed circle sits at the incenter. The circumcenter's circle goes AROUND, through the vertices.

options.label: no circle in particular
options.feedback: It's exactly the circumscribed circle's center — equidistance from the vertices defines it.

tc-circumcenter__mcq.prompt: You want a location equidistant from three towns (treat them as three points). Which triangle center solves this?

options.label: the circumcenter
options.feedback: Equidistant from three POINTS (vertices) is the circumcenter — the perpendicular-bisector meeting point.

options.label: the incenter
options.feedback: The incenter is equidistant from the SIDES, not from three points. For equal distance to points, use the circumcenter.

options.label: the centroid
options.feedback: The centroid is the balance point, not an equal-distance point. Equidistance from vertices is the circumcenter.

options.label: the orthocenter
options.feedback: The orthocenter (altitudes) has no equidistance property. Equal distance from three points is the circumcenter.

tc-cpctc-practice__mcq.prompt: In that proof, the equality BD = BD comes from which reason?

options.label: Reflexive Property (a shared side equals itself)
options.feedback: BD belongs to both triangles, so it equals itself — the reflexive 'free' part that completes the criterion.

options.label: Given
options.feedback: BD = BD isn't stated in the setup — it's SEEN as a shared side and justified as reflexive.

options.label: Definition of angle bisector
options.feedback: That definition gives the equal ANGLES (∠ABD = ∠CBD), not the equal side. BD = BD is reflexive.

options.label: CPCTC
options.feedback: CPCTC comes at the END, after congruence. BD = BD is an input to the criterion, justified by reflexivity.

tc-cpctc-practice__mcq.prompt: To prove two segments in a figure are equal, what is the standard CPCTC strategy?

options.label: Find two triangles containing them as corresponding sides, prove those congruent, then apply CPCTC
options.feedback: Embed the target segments in two triangles, prove congruence by a criterion, and CPCTC releases the equality.

options.label: Measure both segments with a ruler
options.feedback: Measuring proves one case, not a general truth. Use congruent triangles and CPCTC instead.

options.label: Assume they're equal and check later
options.feedback: Assuming the conclusion is circular. Prove the containing triangles congruent, then CPCTC.

options.label: Show the segments are parallel
options.feedback: Parallel isn't equal in length. The route to equal SEGMENTS is congruent triangles + CPCTC.

tc-cpctc-practice__numeric.prompt: △ABC ≅ △DEF is proven, and BC = 9. By CPCTC, what is EF?

commonErrors.feedback: 18 doubles it — congruence keeps sizes equal. BC corresponds to EF, so EF = 9.
4.5 halves it — CPCTC gives EQUAL corresponding parts. EF = BC = 9.

tc-cpctc__mcq.prompt: At what point in a proof may you use CPCTC?

options.label: only after the triangles have been proven congruent
options.feedback: CPCTC extracts equal parts FROM a congruence — so the congruence must be established first.

options.label: as the very first step, to get started
options.feedback: CPCTC needs a congruence to draw from — it can't come before one exists. Prove congruence first.

options.label: any time two triangles share a side
options.feedback: A shared side alone isn't congruence. You must first prove the triangles congruent by a criterion.

options.label: only when using SSS
options.feedback: CPCTC follows ANY criterion (SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS) — not just SSS. It just needs an established congruence.

tc-cpctc__mcq.prompt: Segments AC and BD cross at P, with AP = CP and BP = DP. To prove △APB ≅ △CPD, which criterion applies?

options.label: SAS, using the equal vertical angles at P as the included angle
options.feedback: AP = CP and BP = DP are the two sides; ∠APB = ∠CPD are vertical (equal) — the included angle. That's SAS.

options.label: SSS, using three pairs of equal sides
options.feedback: Only two side pairs are given (AP=CP, BP=DP); the third sides aren't known equal. Use the vertical angle instead: SAS.

options.label: ASA, using two pairs of equal angles
options.feedback: Only ONE angle pair is known (the vertical angles). ASA needs two — here you pair it with two sides: SAS.

options.label: AAS, using the vertical angles and a side
options.feedback: AAS needs TWO angle pairs; you have one angle pair and two sides. The included vertical angle makes it SAS.

tc-cpctc__numeric.prompt: △ABC ≅ △DEF has been proven. If AB = 15, what is DE?

commonErrors.feedback: 30 doubles it — but congruent triangles are the SAME size. Corresponding sides are EQUAL: DE = AB = 15.
7.5 halves it — congruence preserves size exactly. DE corresponds to AB, so DE = 15.

tc-hinge__mcq.prompt: In the hinge theorem, what causes the third side to lengthen?

options.label: Widening the included angle swings the two fixed sides' endpoints farther apart
options.feedback: The two sides stay the same length; opening the angle between them increases the distance across — a longer third side.

options.label: The two given sides get longer
options.feedback: The two sides are FIXED and equal in both triangles — only the ANGLE changes. That's what moves the third side.

options.label: The triangle's area stays constant
options.feedback: Area actually changes as the angle opens, but the KEY driver of the third side is the widening angle itself.

options.label: The third side is always the longest
options.feedback: The third side needn't be longest — the point is it GROWS as the included angle widens.

tc-hinge__mcq.prompt: Two triangles share two pairs of equal sides. Triangle P's third side is longer than Q's. What does the CONVERSE hinge theorem conclude?

options.label: P's included angle is larger than Q's
options.feedback: The converse runs backward: a longer third side means a wider included angle. P's angle is larger.

options.label: P's included angle is smaller than Q's
options.feedback: A longer third side comes from a WIDER angle, not a narrower one — P's angle is larger, not smaller.

options.label: Their included angles are equal
options.feedback: Equal angles would give equal third sides (SAS). Since P's third side is longer, its angle is larger.

options.label: P is congruent to Q
options.feedback: Different third sides rule out congruence. The converse says P's included angle is the larger one.

tc-hinge__mcq.prompt: Triangle X has sides 6 and 9 with a 50° included angle. Triangle Y has sides 6 and 9 with a 70° included angle. Which third side is longer?

options.label: Triangle Y's (70° included angle)
options.feedback: Same two sides, larger included angle (70° > 50°) — Y's third side is longer by the hinge theorem.

options.label: Triangle X's (50° included angle)
options.feedback: The smaller angle makes the SHORTER third side. Y's wider 70° angle gives the longer one.

options.label: They are equal
options.feedback: Equal only if the included angles matched — but 50° ≠ 70°, so Y's third side is longer.

options.label: Cannot be determined
options.feedback: It can: the sides are identical, so the larger included angle (Y) determines the longer third side.

tc-hl__mcq.prompt: SSA usually fails, so why does HL (which looks similar) succeed?

options.label: The right angle lets the Pythagorean theorem fix the second leg to one value
options.feedback: With the right angle known, a² + b² = c² determines the missing leg uniquely — no swinging, no second triangle.

options.label: HL uses three sides like SSS
options.feedback: HL gives a right angle, a hypotenuse, and ONE leg — not three sides. The right angle is what removes the ambiguity.

options.label: Right triangles are always congruent
options.feedback: Right triangles vary widely — HL congruence needs the equal hypotenuse and leg. The right angle just fixes the third side.

options.label: HL only works for isosceles triangles
options.feedback: HL applies to any right triangle, isosceles or not — the key is the right angle plus hypotenuse and a leg.

tc-hl__mcq.prompt: Two right triangles each have hypotenuse 10 and one leg 6. What can you conclude?

options.label: They are congruent by HL
options.feedback: Right angle, equal hypotenuse (10), equal leg (6) — the HL criterion gives congruence.

options.label: They are congruent by SSA
options.feedback: SSA isn't a valid criterion. Because these are RIGHT triangles with hypotenuse and leg, the correct name is HL.

options.label: They might not be congruent
options.feedback: With the right angle fixed, the other leg is forced (√(100−36)=8) — the triangles must be congruent by HL.

options.label: They are only similar
options.feedback: Equal hypotenuse AND leg fix the size, not just the shape — congruent by HL, not merely similar.

tc-hl__numeric.prompt: Two right triangles each have hypotenuse 17 and one leg 8. What is the length of the other leg in each?

commonErrors.feedback: 9 = 17 − 8 subtracts the sides. Use squares: √(17² − 8²) = √225 = 15.
25 = 17 + 8 adds them. The other leg is √(17² − 8²) = √(289 − 64) = 15.

tc-incenter__mcq.prompt: The incenter is the center of…

options.label: the inscribed circle, which touches all three sides
options.feedback: Equal distance to each side is the radius of the circle nestled inside, touching all three — the incircle.

options.label: the circle through the three vertices
options.feedback: That's the circumscribed circle at the CIRCUMCENTER. The incenter's circle touches the SIDES from inside.

options.label: a circle centered at a vertex
options.feedback: The incenter sits INSIDE the triangle, not at a vertex — it centers the inscribed circle.

options.label: no circle at all
options.feedback: It's precisely the inscribed circle's center — equidistance from the sides gives that circle's radius.

tc-inequality-proofs__mcq.prompt: In △ABC with a = 10, b = 7, c = 5, order the angles from smallest to largest.

options.label: ∠C < ∠B < ∠A
options.feedback: Each angle matches its opposite side: c=5 → ∠C smallest, b=7 → ∠B middle, a=10 → ∠A largest.

options.label: ∠A < ∠B < ∠C
options.feedback: That reverses it — ∠A is opposite the LONGEST side (10), so ∠A is LARGEST, not smallest.

options.label: ∠B < ∠A < ∠C
options.feedback: Order the opposite sides instead: 5 < 7 < 10 gives ∠C < ∠B < ∠A.

options.label: they cannot be ordered
options.feedback: They can — angle order matches opposite-side order: ∠C < ∠B < ∠A.

tc-inequality-proofs__mcq.prompt: Why is a triangle's exterior angle greater than either remote interior angle?

options.label: It equals their sum, so it exceeds each one individually
options.feedback: The exterior angle is the sum of both remote interiors — adding a positive angle makes it larger than either alone.

options.label: Because exterior angles are always obtuse
options.feedback: Exterior angles can be acute (e.g., remote interiors 20° and 30° give 50°). It exceeds each remote interior because it's their SUM.

options.label: Because it is supplementary to them
options.feedback: It's supplementary to the ADJACENT interior angle, not the remote ones. It EQUALS the sum of the remotes.

options.label: Because all exterior angles are equal
options.feedback: Exterior angles vary. Each exceeds its remote interiors because it equals their sum.

tc-inequality-proofs__mcq.prompt: Two triangles share sides of length 8 and 11. The included angle in the first is 65°, in the second 50°. To prove the first's third side is longer, which theorem do you cite?

options.label: the hinge theorem (larger included angle ⇒ longer third side)
options.feedback: Same two sides, and 65° > 50°, so the hinge theorem gives the first triangle the longer third side.

options.label: the triangle inequality
options.feedback: The triangle inequality tests whether sides form a triangle — it doesn't COMPARE two triangles' third sides. Use the hinge.

options.label: the base angles theorem
options.feedback: That's about isosceles triangles' equal angles, not comparing third sides. The hinge theorem applies here.

options.label: SAS congruence
options.feedback: The included angles DIFFER (65° ≠ 50°), so it's not congruence — it's the hinge INEQUALITY.

tc-isosceles-converse__mcq.prompt: You measure two angles of a triangle and find them equal. By the converse, what follows?

options.label: The sides opposite those angles are equal, so the triangle is isosceles
options.feedback: Equal angles ⇒ equal opposite sides — the converse gives you an isosceles triangle.

options.label: The third angle is also equal
options.feedback: Two equal angles don't force the third — that would be equilateral. The converse gives equal SIDES.

options.label: The triangle is right-angled
options.feedback: Equal angles don't imply a right angle. They imply equal opposite sides — isosceles.

options.label: Nothing — you need the sides
options.feedback: The converse is exactly what lets angles conclude equal SIDES. You don't need to measure them.

tc-isosceles-converse__mcq.prompt: A triangle has all three sides equal. What can you conclude about its angles?

options.label: All three angles are equal, each 60°
options.feedback: Applying the Base Angles Theorem to each side pair makes every angle equal; 180 ÷ 3 = 60°.

options.label: The angles could be any sizes
options.feedback: Equal sides force equal angles — they can't vary. Each is exactly 60°.

options.label: Only two angles are equal
options.feedback: That's isosceles. With ALL sides equal, ALL three angles are equal — 60° each.

options.label: One angle must be 90°
options.feedback: An equilateral triangle has no right angle; all three angles are 60°.

tc-isosceles-converse__numeric.prompt: A triangle has two base angles measuring (3x)° and (2x + 20)°, and they are equal. Find the measure of each base angle, in degrees.

commonErrors.feedback: 20 is the value of x, not the angle. Substitute: 3(20) = 60°.
100 comes from adding the two expressions. They're EQUAL (3x = 2x + 20 → x = 20), so each is 3(20) = 60°.

tc-isosceles__mcq.prompt: What construction proves the base angles equal?

options.label: Bisect the apex angle, creating two triangles congruent by SAS
options.feedback: The bisector gives equal half-angles, the legs are equal, and the bisector is shared — SAS congruence, then CPCTC equates the base angles.

options.label: Measure both base angles with a protractor
options.feedback: Measuring checks one triangle, not all — the theorem needs a proof. The apex bisector gives SAS congruence.

options.label: Draw a circle through all three vertices
options.feedback: A circumscribed circle doesn't directly equate the base angles. The apex-angle bisector and SAS do.

options.label: Assume the base angles are equal
options.feedback: Assuming the conclusion is circular. The bisector-plus-SAS argument derives it.

tc-isosceles__numeric.prompt: An isosceles triangle has base angles of 65° each. What is its apex angle, in degrees?

commonErrors.feedback: 65° is a BASE angle. The apex is what's left after both base angles: 180 − 65 − 65 = 50°.
115 = 180 − 65 subtracts only ONE base angle. Subtract both: 180 − 130 = 50°.

tc-isosceles__numeric.prompt: An isosceles triangle has an apex angle of 50°. One base angle is labeled (5x)°. Find x.

commonErrors.feedback: 65 is the base ANGLE in degrees, not x. Since 5x = 65, divide: x = 13.
10 would make 5x = 50, the APEX angle — but 5x is a BASE angle = 65, so x = 13.

tc-midsegment__mcq.prompt: A midsegment of a triangle is guaranteed to be…

options.label: parallel to the third side and half its length
options.feedback: Both properties come together: the midsegment parallels the third side and is exactly half as long.

options.label: perpendicular to the third side
options.feedback: It's PARALLEL to the third side, not perpendicular — they never meet at a right angle in general.

options.label: equal in length to the third side
options.feedback: It's HALF the third side, not equal — joining midpoints shrinks it by exactly a factor of two.

options.label: half the length but not parallel
options.feedback: It's half AND parallel — both hold. The parallelism is as guaranteed as the halving.

tc-midsegment__numeric.prompt: A triangle has perimeter 24. Connecting all three side-midpoints forms a smaller triangle. What is its perimeter?

commonErrors.feedback: 24 is the ORIGINAL perimeter. Each midsegment is half a side, so the inner perimeter is half: 24 ÷ 2 = 12.
48 doubles it — the midpoint triangle is SMALLER. Each side halves, so the perimeter is 24 ÷ 2 = 12.

tc-midsegment__numeric.fallbackFeedback: Each side halves, so the perimeter halves: 24 ÷ 2 = 12.

tc-midsegment__numeric.prompt: A midsegment measures (2x + 1) and the side it's parallel to measures 22. Find x.

commonErrors.feedback: 11 is the midsegment's LENGTH (half of 22), not x. Since 2x + 1 = 11, solve: x = 5.
10.5 = 22/2 − … miscomputes. The midsegment is 22 ÷ 2 = 11, so 2x + 1 = 11 gives x = 5.

tc-overlapping__mcq.prompt: Why redraw overlapping triangles as two separate triangles?

options.label: To see the corresponding parts clearly and match them to a criterion
options.feedback: Separation exposes which sides and angles correspond — including the shared reflexive part — so a criterion can be applied.

options.label: Because overlapping triangles aren't real triangles
options.feedback: They're perfectly real — separating them is just a clarity trick, not a fix for something invalid.

options.label: To make the figure larger
options.feedback: Size isn't the point; visibility of corresponding parts is. Separation clarifies the correspondence.

options.label: Because CPCTC requires separate drawings
options.feedback: CPCTC doesn't require redrawing — separating is an optional aid to spot corresponding parts.

tc-overlapping__mcq.prompt: In a two-congruence proof, what links the first congruence to the second?

options.label: A part obtained by CPCTC from the first becomes an input to the second
options.feedback: The first CPCTC hands you an equal part, which you then use to prove the second pair congruent.

options.label: The second proof ignores the first
options.feedback: They're linked precisely because the first CPCTC supplies a part the second proof needs.

options.label: Both proofs must use SSS
options.feedback: Either proof can use any criterion — the link is the shared part from CPCTC, not a fixed criterion.

options.label: The two triangles must be identical
options.feedback: They're different triangles; what connects the stages is the CPCTC part passed between them.

tc-overlapping__mcq.prompt: Two overlapping triangles share vertex angle ∠A, and the two sides forming ∠A are equal in each. Which criterion proves them congruent?

options.label: SAS, with the shared ∠A as the included angle
options.feedback: The common angle ∠A equals itself (reflexive) and sits between the two equal sides — that's SAS.

options.label: ASA, using two shared angles
options.feedback: Only ONE angle (∠A) is shared. With two SIDES around it, the pattern is SAS, not ASA.

options.label: SSS, using three shared sides
options.feedback: Only two sides are known equal here; the shared ∠A supplies the third part. That's SAS.

options.label: HL, using a hypotenuse
options.feedback: There's no right angle stated here — the shared angle with two sides gives SAS.

tc-sas__mcq.prompt: Two triangles have two pairs of equal sides, and the angles BETWEEN those sides are equal. Which criterion applies?

options.label: SAS
options.feedback: Two sides with the included angle between them — side-angle-side.

options.label: SSA
options.feedback: SSA would be two sides and a NON-included angle — and that one doesn't guarantee congruence. Here the angle is included: SAS.

options.label: ASA
options.feedback: ASA is two ANGLES with the side between them. Here you have two SIDES with the angle between: SAS.

options.label: SSS
options.feedback: SSS needs three equal SIDES. Here only two sides plus the included angle are given: SAS.

tc-ssa-fails__mcq.prompt: What makes SSA fail where SAS succeeds?

options.label: SSA's angle is NOT between the two sides, so a side can swing to two positions
options.feedback: The non-included angle lets the opposite side reach two points — two triangles. SAS's included angle allows only one.

options.label: SSA uses angles and SAS uses sides
options.feedback: Both use two sides and one angle — the difference is the angle's POSITION: included (SAS) vs not (SSA).

options.label: SSA triangles are always larger
options.feedback: Size isn't the issue — it's that SSA can produce two DIFFERENT triangles from one set of parts.

options.label: SAS is newer than SSA
options.feedback: Neither is 'newer' — SAS works and SSA doesn't because of where the angle sits relative to the sides.

tc-ssa-fails__mcq.prompt: A triangle and a copy twice as large have the same three angles. They are…

options.label: similar but not congruent
options.feedback: Same angles → same shape → similar; the doubled size breaks congruence.

options.label: congruent
options.feedback: Congruent triangles are the SAME size. Doubling the copy makes them similar, not congruent.

options.label: neither similar nor congruent
options.feedback: They ARE similar — identical angles guarantee same shape. They just aren't congruent.

options.label: congruent only if right triangles
options.feedback: Right or not, a doubled copy is similar, never congruent — the sizes differ.

tc-ssa-fails__mcq.prompt: Which of these does NOT guarantee two triangles are congruent?

options.label: SSA — two sides and a non-included angle
options.feedback: SSA is the ambiguous case — one set of parts, potentially two triangles. Not a valid criterion.

options.label: SAS — two sides and the included angle
options.feedback: SAS is valid: the included angle locks the third side to one length.

options.label: ASA — two angles and the included side
options.feedback: ASA is valid: two angles and the side between them fix the triangle.

options.label: AAS — two angles and a non-included side
options.feedback: AAS is valid: the angle sum recovers the third angle, reducing it to ASA.

tc-sss__mcq.prompt: Why does SSS (three pairs of equal sides) guarantee congruence?

options.label: Three side lengths determine a triangle's shape completely — the angles are forced
options.feedback: With all three sides fixed there's exactly one triangle (up to a rigid motion), so the angles can't differ.

options.label: Because three is more than two
options.feedback: It's not about the COUNT being big — it's that three sides leave no freedom. Two sides alone wouldn't fix the shape.

options.label: Because sides are more important than angles
options.feedback: Neither is 'more important' — it's that fixing all three sides happens to force the angles too.

options.label: Because every triangle has three sides
options.feedback: True but beside the point — the reason is that three EQUAL sides pin down one unique shape.

tc-triangle-inequality__mcq.prompt: What's the fastest way to test whether three lengths form a triangle?

options.label: Check that the two shortest sides sum to more than the longest
options.feedback: The two smallest summing past the largest is the hardest condition — if it holds, the triangle is valid.

options.label: Check that the two longest sides sum to more than the shortest
options.feedback: That's the EASIEST pairing and almost always passes — it doesn't catch failures. Test the two SHORTEST vs the longest.

options.label: Add all three sides and compare to 180
options.feedback: 180 is about ANGLES, not side lengths. Compare the two shortest sides' sum to the longest side.

options.label: Check that all three sides are equal
options.feedback: Triangles needn't be equilateral. The test is the two shortest sides exceeding the longest.

tc-triangle-inequality__numeric.prompt: With two sides 5 and 8, the third side must be GREATER than what value?

commonErrors.feedback: 13 is the UPPER bound (5 + 8) — the third must be LESS than that. The lower bound is the DIFFERENCE: 8 − 5 = 3.
0 is too weak — a side of length 2 would fail (2 + 5 < 8). The real floor is |8 − 5| = 3.

tc-triangle-inequality__numeric.prompt: Two sides of a triangle are 7 and 10. How many INTEGER values are possible for the third side?

commonErrors.feedback: 14 counts 3 through 16 — but the third side must be strictly GREATER than 3, so start at 4: values 4 through 16 = 13.
17 is the upper bound itself, which is excluded. Integers strictly between 3 and 17 are 4 through 16 = 13.
